tagline: Follow Willow Creek through wheat country, then climb into pine and fir
intro: The Blue Mountain Scenic Byway follows Willow Creek through wheat and canola fields before climbing into the pine and fir of Umatilla National Forest. Oregon’s transportation department presents this scenic byway as an alternative to I-84, with historic towns and outdoor recreation along its eastern leg. TripCheck gives a minimum driving time of three to four hours. Ione and Lexington began as sheep stations, and TripCheck points out their surviving examples of frontier architecture.

The Willow Creek corridor carried travelers before the scenic drive: the Oregon Trail crossed the creek at Cecil, which also became a stagecoach stop. In 1888, the Oregon Railroad and Navigation Company completed a spur up the drainage to Heppner. By the early twentieth century, the railway and expanding road network had made Heppner a distribution point for farm products, from wheat and alfalfa to sheep and cattle.

Start at Heppner Junction off I-84, following OR 74 through Ione and Lexington to Heppner. Beyond Heppner, Willow Creek Road leads into the forest; the byway then descends into Ukiah’s ancient lake basin. Another climb brings Bridge Creek Wildlife Area before the eastern portal at North Fork John Day Campground, where the route meets the Elkhorn Drive Scenic Byway.

moments.title: Heppner
moments.text: Heppner’s courthouse owes its survival in the 1903 flood partly to its elevated site. County officials moved into the new building in March; the flash flood struck Willow Creek in June. The courthouse uses locally quarried dark blue basalt with lighter trim stone from near Elgin and Baker. Built in 1902–03, the courthouse replaced an earlier wooden courthouse. A domed cupola carries clock faces on three sides. The Morrow County Museum chronicles the flood alongside its collections of homestead and rural history, giving the disaster a place within the town’s longer story.
moments.notice: Dark blue basalt and pale trim distinguish the courthouse; its cupola has clocks on three sides.

moments.title: Ukiah
moments.text: At Ukiah, the byway descends out of the forest into an ancient lake basin. In spring, bright blue camas flowers grow here in abundance. The Camas Land Company platted the town in August 1890, and a post office opened the following month. Its name came from E. B. Gambee, who had moved from Ukiah, California. Camas Creek flows west from the Blue Mountains through Umatilla National Forest and past the town, continuing as a tributary of the North Fork John Day River. The town stands at the junction of US 395 and Oregon Route 244.
moments.notice: Bright blue camas flowers are a spring feature of Ukiah’s basin.

moments.title: Bridge Creek Wildlife Area
moments.text: Bridge Creek Wildlife Area is winter country for Rocky Mountain elk. TripCheck identifies it as a wintering ground for one of the nation’s largest herds, reached after the byway climbs back into the forest beyond Ukiah. A short trail provides a viewpoint over the wintering grounds. The transportation department gives December through May as the best period for seeing elk, while also warning that winter snow closes the byway at higher elevations.
